## HOOK
[VISUAL: night drone shot of the Theodosian Walls, slow push-in]
For a thousand years, these walls protected the richest city in the Christian world. Armies came from every direction, including Avars, Arabs, Bulgars and Rus, and every one of them failed to break through them by force. Then, in the spring of 1453, a twenty-one-year-old sultan broke through them in just fifty-three days. How did a wall that had never been broken by force collapse so quickly, and what did it cost the people who lived behind it?

## PROMISE
In this video, we'll look at the city of Constantinople, the young sultan Mehmed II, the last emperor Constantine XI, the giant cannon that changed siege warfare, and the extraordinary trick that put an Ottoman fleet inside a harbour that was supposed to be sealed. By the end, you'll understand why 1453 is often seen as the end of the Middle Ages.

## CONTEXT
Constantinople was founded by the Roman emperor Constantine the Great in 330 AD as a new capital for the Roman Empire. Over the following centuries, the western half of the empire collapsed, but the eastern half, which historians call the Byzantine Empire, survived and continued for roughly another thousand years. The city was protected by water on three sides and by the Theodosian Walls on the fourth, a system of moat, outer wall and inner wall stretching around 5.7 kilometres from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn, which was constructed in the fifth century under Emperor Theodosius II. By 1453, however, the empire had shrunk dramatically and was little more than the city itself and a few scattered territories, and the population of the city had fallen to perhaps fifty thousand people.

Meanwhile, the Ottoman Turks had expanded across Anatolia and the Balkans and had surrounded the city on almost every side. In 1451, Mehmed II became sultan at the age of eighteen, and he decided that taking Constantinople would be the defining act of his reign. He built a fortress called Rumeli Hisari on the European side of the Bosphorus in 1452 to control shipping, and then he started preparing his army.

## CHAPTER 1
And then a Hungarian engineer named Orban arrived. Orban was a founder who specialised in casting large bronze cannons. He first offered his services to the Byzantine emperor, but Constantine could not afford to pay him what he wanted, and so Orban went to Mehmed instead, who paid him far more than he had asked for and gave him all the materials he needed. Orban then built an enormous cannon, reportedly around eight metres long, capable of firing a stone ball weighing several hundred kilograms more than a mile. It took sixty oxen and hundreds of men to move it into position in front of the walls. And then on 6 April 1453 the siege began, and the bombardment continued every day for weeks. The cannon could only fire a few times a day because it needed to cool down, but each impact smashed sections of the outer wall, and the defenders worked through the night to repair the damage with timber, earth and barrels.

## TURNING POINT
And then, on 22 April, the defenders woke up to an incredible sight. The Byzantines had stretched a massive chain across the entrance of the Golden Horn, so the Ottoman fleet could not get in. But Mehmed ordered his men to build a road of greased logs behind the Genoese colony of Galata, and they dragged around seventy ships over the hill and into the harbour. Now the city had to defend its sea walls as well, and the already small garrison of about seven thousand men was stretched even thinner. Then, in the early hours of 29 May, the final assault began. The Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried away from the walls, and the defenders started to panic. Ottoman soldiers broke through, and Constantine XI was killed in the fighting, although his body was never identified.

## CLOSE
The fall of Constantinople ended the Byzantine Empire and turned the city into the new Ottoman capital, later known as Istanbul. It also showed that gunpowder artillery could defeat even the strongest medieval walls, and it encouraged many Greek scholars to move west to Italy, contributing to the Renaissance.
